author_or_org: Wensu Li, Atin Aboutorabi, Harry Lyu, Kaizhi Qian, Martin Fleming, Brian C. Goehring, Neil Thompson

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: The paper models automation intensity as a continuous choice from no automation through partial human-AI collaboration to full automation, rather than as a binary automate-or-not decision.
claims.quote: Moving beyond binary automate-or-not assessments, we model automation intensity as a continuous choice in which firms minimize costs by selecting an AI accuracy level, from no automation through partial human-AI collaboration to full automation.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: Because AI systems show predictable but diminishing returns to data, compute, and model size, the cost of higher accuracy is convex: good performance may be cheap, but near-perfect accuracy is disproportionately expensive.
claims.quote: Because AI systems exhibit predictable but diminishing returns to these inputs, the cost of higher accuracy is convex: good performance may be inexpensive, but near-perfect accuracy is disproportionately costly.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: Full automation is often not cost-minimizing, and partial automation where humans retain residual tasks frequently emerges as the equilibrium.
claims.quote: Full automation is therefore often not cost-minimizing; partial automation, where firms retain human workers for residual tasks, frequently emerges as the equilibrium.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: Task complexity shapes labor substitution: low-complexity tasks see high substitution, while high-complexity tasks favor limited partial automation.
claims.quote: Task complexity shapes substitution: low-complexity tasks see high substitution, while high-complexity tasks favor limited partial automation.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: Scale of deployment is a key determinant because AI-as-a-Service and AI agents spread fixed costs across users and sharply expand economically viable tasks.
claims.quote: Scale of deployment is a key determinant: AI-as-a-Service and AI agents spread fixed costs across users, sharply expanding economically viable tasks.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: At the firm level, cost-effective automation captures approximately 11% of computer-vision-exposed labor compensation, and this share rises sharply under economy-wide deployment.
claims.quote: At the firm level, cost-effective automation captures approximately 11% of computer-vision-exposed labor compensation; under economy-wide deployment, this share rises sharply.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: The paper argues that partial automation is often the economically rational long-run outcome, not merely a transitional phase, because other AI systems exhibit similar scaling-law economics.
claims.quote: Since other AI systems exhibit similar scaling-law economics, our mechanisms extend beyond computer vision, reinforcing that partial automation is often the economically rational long-run outcome, not merely a transitional phase.
